claims.text: Formation and retention of a protective oxide layer are primarily governed by preferential diffusion and surface segregation of Cr or Al.
Surface-segregated Cr or Al forms a continuous, adherent oxide scale during oxidation.
The initial high-entropy alloy has a homogeneous distribution of multiple principal elements, including Cr or Al.
Nanoscale compositional fluctuations enhance the surface concentration of Cr or Al.
At elevated temperatures, high-entropy effects accelerate diffusion kinetics.
Accelerated diffusion promotes migration and surface segregation of Cr or Al.
Segregated Cr or Al reacts with oxygen to form a dense, adherent oxide scale.
The dense, adherent oxide scale limits further oxidation of the bulk alloy.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the high-entropy alloy will develop a thicker oxide layer.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the high-entropy alloy will develop a more uniform and protective oxide layer.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the high-entropy alloy will exhibit lower mass gain during oxidation.
Suppressing high-entropy-induced diffusion or refractory-element segregation reduces protective oxide-scale formation.
The proposed mechanism dominates when temperature and oxygen partial pressure are sufficient to drive rapid diffusion and oxidation.
The proposed effect may be diminished or altered at lower temperatures or under atypical oxygen conditions.
